item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: God differentiated hundreds of species of finches in the Galapagos because it makes him angry when we put it in the butt. If A, then B, it’s simple logic people. Of course in more recent times than the 6000 years ago when the earth was created, books actually attributable to their authors would declare God [...]
item.content:encoded:
God differentiated hundreds of species of finches in the Galapagos because it makes him angry when we put it in the butt.  If A, then B, it’s simple logic people.

Dinosaurs and people, together in harmony

Of course in more recent times than the 6000 years ago when the earth was created, books actually attributable to their authors would declare God is dead, so I guess it’s all a matter of what you choose to believe.  And at the Creation Museum in Florence Kentucky, judging by the fact it’s run by an organization called Origins In Genesis, what they believe is pretty clear.

For anyone who’s seen Religulous where Bill Maher visits and rightfully skewers the place, well, it’s exactly as he described.  Man and dinosaur living together as one, the entire earth actually being covered by the great flood, plenty of goofy placards explaining why man knows nothing beyond the unquestionable word of God in the Bible, how modern society is descending into sin, all that fun stuff.

Gotta get 'em while they're young

Funny thing is, I wasn’t really bothered by all of it, not that I expected I’d start yelling at random people that the Bible is fiction and they are all insane, but it was kind of a pleasant place.  Everyone who worked there was really friendly, the exhibits did mention things like the big bang, evolution and plate techtonics, just that they were wrong because they weren’t in the Bible.  It was kind of quirky and cute, really.

There were also really nice grounds and a petting zoo, although I skipped that part.  However, Phase 2 of the museum is to build a life-sized recreation of Noah’s Arc, and if you donate now you can get a ticket in case flood number two happens!  Sounds like money well spent to me!

Here’s the gallery.

item.title: The Kentucky Bourbon Trail
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: I’ve always enjoyed bourbon in the sense that drinking it makes you feel like a down home country gentleman, even if you’re mixing it with coke just to get (sour) mashed (which means a small portion of the previous fermentation is added to a new batch to speed the process). item.content:encoded:
Delish

I’ve always enjoyed bourbon in the sense that drinking it makes you feel like a down home country gentleman, even if you’re mixing it with coke just to get (sour) mashed (which means a small portion of the previous fermentation is added to a new batch to speed the process).  There’s even a reason for this statesman-like quality as bourbon was marketed as the drink of the modern aristocrat once American beer consumption overtook that of spirits in the 1800′s.  However, now that I’ve been through half of the bourbon trail in Kentucky where 95% of the world’s supply is distilled, I might just start enjoying a glass on its own from time to time.

You see, bourbon is no different than Scotch or Irish whiskey, it’s just the ratio of the grains that are fermented, what type of barrel they are aged in, and for how long.  In fact, most of the original crafters of bourbon were all of Scottish or Irish decent, corn just happens to be in abundance in America, and there still is rye, wheat or barley mixed in depending on which brand you’re tasting.  Some of the used bourbon barrels are even sent to the UK these days for re-use in whiskey aging because due to one of those funny jurisdictional classification laws like Champagne or Agave Tequila, Kentucky Bourbon can only be crafted from a barrel made of freshly charred, virgin oak.

One of those “funny laws” that really makes a difference as it pertains to Kentucky is the water here.  Central Kentucky, where all the distilleries are located within 100 miles of eachother, lies on a bed of limestone that naturally filters the water causing it to have a high calcium, low iron content and generally be free of contaminants, which is what gives bourbon it’s clean, smooth taste.  Clean and smooth is what I have been conditioned to say after all the tourism videos at the distillery tours, it’s still goddam whiskey for Christ’s sake.

However, it could be worse.  I learned the term “gut rot” originated from a type of whiskey/moonshine that used to have lead additivites that made it taste so smooth and sweet you would only want that type of whiskey, until you died because your stomach lining and intestinal tract were dead from lead poisoning.  Or even better, to seal up whiskey barrels, naturally there’s a small hole, into which a small stopper is hammered into place, the stopper being called the bung.  And so where does the stopper get stuck into?  The bung hole!  Beavis and Butthead must have been bourbon fans.

Anyways, history aside, I always used to drink Wild Turkey because it’s prevalent, cheap, and has a turkey on the bottle, but I don’t believe I ever will again (OK, that’s a lie for effect, blow me).  Not only was their tour the most homogenized vanilla crap of any due to their ownership by a giant multinational liquor conglormerate, the stuff also tasted like swill…and when I say vanilla crap, I mean it, there’s actually vanillan extract inside oak wood.

Naturally all the tours end with a fine tasting of the better than average stuff they want you to buy, but the Wild Turkey Rare Breed and all the other bullshit they were hocking were awful.  To make matters worse, on account of their multinational ownership, they were the only distillery I visited that sends all their alcohol to somewhere random in Arkansas to be bottled, not on site.

I could go on at great length about how the suspended solids in bourbon adhere to ice, why it should be put in the refridgerator, not room temperature or the freezer prior to serving and how the location of the barrel inside the….oh, OK, that one’s really cool.  You know how a good Scotch will be something like a 23 year old, whereas a good bourbon can be found in the 10 year range?  The reason is the temperature in Kentucky.  Because it gets so much hotter here in the summer, more of the liquid in the barrel will be forced into the wood, only to be sucked back out in the sub-zero winter temperatures, thereby absorbing more flavour in less time.  That’s also why which storey on the 7, sometimes 8 tall warehouses the barrel is stored will affect whether it winds up a in a blended or small batch final product, versus the eponymous “single barrel”, which are the ones aged in what they call the “honey spots” because it gets so much hotter on the top floors.

And, because wood is pourous and water molecules are smaller than alcohol, a batch that starts at 120 proof could easily end up at 130 proof.  The entire warehouse smells distinctly of bourbon because of this leakage, which is roughly 3% a year and called the “angel’s share”, so some of the very expensive craft bourbons aged over 20 years wind up being removed with a barrel that’s half full.  And on of the main reason’s they’re so expensive is because bourbon sitting on the shelf aging is taxed every year regardless to the tune of half of the state of Kentucky’s revenue!

Uhhh, I need to stop.  The answer to the ultimate question is Eagle Rare Single Barrel, trust me.  It’s $27 in Kentucky and $60 in Canada, so I just need to convert Bessie into a bootlegging machine and I’m good to go.

Check the gallery for some behind-the-scenes shots of how bourbon works.

item.title: Best. Comment. Ever.
item.dc:creator: Blimpy
item.description: 3 months between posts is no way to run a blog, but I’ve been awoken by a most excellent comment on a post I made about Crescent City CA almost two years ago. It’s moment like this that make me glad the content I previously posted is just sitting there on the interwebs for all [...]
item.content:encoded:
3 months between posts is no way to run a blog, but I’ve been awoken by a most excellent comment on a post I made about Crescent City CA almost two years ago.  It’s moment like this that make me glad the content I previously posted is just sitting there on the interwebs for all to see and write their take on.

I’ve been living in Memphis for the last 4 months and very soon should update people on the unique structure of this city versus the yuppie paradise I grew up in, post some pictures of the dope garden I am growing or some of the excellent BBQ I’ve been eating.  I’ve held off because it just doesn’t feel the same as when I was trudging across the continent, me and Bessie versus the world.  But regardless, I have reposted the comment from Tracy as well as my response below and for now have miraculously held of on writing more because I believe it all speaks for itself.  Enjoy.

Tracy’s comment:

I have lived in Crescent city and Brookings. And believe me when I say that we are very happy to see narrow minded, communist, Obama loving, vegan burger eating people like you drive right through. Yes it is correct that we have tradional ways and still stand for the US constitution that our old outdated forfathers wrote. If you want to live in a modern more communist like soiciety then move to China or Germany. We like our right to keep and bear arms, our right to freedom of speech. I know your type likes to be told what to do and eat and how to do it by Big Brother. The truth is it’s your type that is killing the good old USA by taking away basic family structure and moral values, by killing us slowly with political correctness, by tieing up all our jobs with inviromental BS. If it wasn’t for you and your type we would still be a manufacturing nation that thrives on it’s own natural resources like wood, oil, farmland and gold ect. Instead we depend on China for almost everything. So really….keep driving!

My reply:

Thanks for writing Tracy! I’m going to dedicate an entire post to your great feedback, I just wanted to clarify a few things first:

-I’m not narrow minded, communist, Obama loving or vegan. One could argue bundling all those terms together in a blanket negative light would make you guilty of the first.

-You mention a modern communist “soiciety” such as Germany, but they actually practice capitalism there.

-I am able to choose my own meals without the help of Big Brother.

-You blame “your type” (i.e. me) for “tieing up all our jobs with inviromental BS” then are upset the US is not thriving due to it’s natural resources such as oil and gold. There is a limited amount of those things in the ground and when they run out we have to a) import them from other countries and b) alter our consumption and manufacturing patterns…it’s not related to the “type” of person you or I represent.

I could go on, but am hoping (likely in vein) to hear more from you soon!

The fridge broke, but other than that the old [...]
item.content:encoded:
After spending the last month in Memphis, it apparently became time for a brief weekend saunter to a campground outside of town for a lil’ break and to make sure Bessie still works, so off I went the nearest State Park an hour away in Arkansas.  The fridge broke, but other than that the old girl is still holding up fine…

My fire poker, which is actually the size of my pinky

With Forrest City being the town closest to the park (and possessing a Walmart for supplies…hell, it’s Arkansas, Walmart is a landmark), the name immediately conjured up images of oak trees and owls nestled around pristine lakes and rivers.  While this may indeed by the case, it’s a funny thing how one extra R in Forrest changes the meaning greatly.  Yes, that would be Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Civil War general and founding member of the KKK, there’s a giant statue of him in Nashville too, but you know, this is the South, so they’re clearly only revering his Civil War tactical mastery and nothing else and if you say any different you better shut your mouth.  I’m not sure if the fact there’s a majority black population is Forrest City is funny, ironic or something I shouldn’t be talking about.

Back at the zoo in Memphis

I had seen Arkansas more than once as I trudged up the Mississippi Delta in November, but honestly had no intention of ever crossing the river.  I won’t be visiting any major cities or interacting with many locals in the forest, so I’ll have to reserve judgement, but…it seems nice?  Bill Clinton is from here, he’s a man.  And as a random aside, over the last four weeks I have met two different people who mentioned they had visited all 50 states.  Why anyone would do that is beyond me (apologies to South Dakota and Nebraska) and considering I’ve only been to 13 states in the last year and a half, I don’t want to be driving around until 2017 just to say I saw Mt. Rushmore.  Or do I…?

Regardless, to kill time at the campground I busted out the old extension tubes for the camera lens and took a few macro shots, and tagged on some from the Memphis zoo to make the gallery.

item.dc:creator: Blimpy

item.content:encoded:
Well, that weekend was bat shit insane.  I’m also astonished I made it out relatively unscathed.  It’s also one of the few times you’ll ever hear me say this about anything…believe the hype.

Without going way overboard on tales of bohemian fascination, the immense character of the city, that everyone will have a “New Orleans moment” and it’s way safer than advertized plus you can drink on the street, well, all those things are true.  And beads and parade floats and costumes and brass bands and genuine people everywhere, both locals and tourists.

Hundreds of floats like this all weekend

After being somewhat terrified at the Muses parade Thursday realizing it was a whole weekend of that, except many thousands more people, I got in the swing quick.  Thursday was also the only day I bothered to venture out with my actual camera, so that gallery is here (not that pictures do it any justice).

On Friday after proclaiming the day before I wasn’t really big into parades, there I was back again near the start of the route in the garden district jumping up and down like a school girl waving to people on the floats for throws (my total count for the weekend was around 25 strings of beads, 2 footballs, 1 frisbee and 1 plastic cup, and I wasn’t trying).  Wandering up Magazine, or maybe Tchoupitoulas, I stopped to chat with a bunch of kids my age who lived in a house right on the parade route.  Within minutes the high fives, dance moves, and handle of Jack Daniels being passed around were all flowing freely.  I was aided in making fast friends because one of the residents had lived in Saskatchewan at some point, so got Canadian props.  Eventually I sheepishly asked to use his bathroom as those are coveted like nothing else on the parade route, then I found I never really left the house once the full drum kit and guitars came out for jamming and the bong started going around, then I have no idea what happened because I forgot to eat dinner, but I made it back to Bessie alright although I must have fallen down a few times.

Sexy shiny dancers

Saturday poured rain, I won’t bore you with the details of that or Sunday, but Monday, a.k.a. Lundi Gras is the big party day.  The cops even show up on Bourbon Street at midnight to clear everybody out, I only made it over there once and it’s not my crowd, there’s so many better places and cheaper bars with more character.  Like for example, Parasol’s, rumoured to be where the Po’Boy was first invented and open since the 1950’s.  It was there dealing with the one and a half hour wait for two sandwiches with a friend I’d made earlier in the week that we met Frank and Leroy…

Sitting on a sunny stoop across the street as every table was full, a man in his 50s with wild wavy hair and a sequined Mardi Gras visor came over in his wheelchair and informed us he called this “the office” because he’d always sit there and drink with his acquaintances, which was every single person who walked by.  Having been diagnosed with MS a few years earlier definitely didn’t slow Frank down, in fact it probably sped him up thanks to her service dog Leroy, a beautiful and friendly red lab.  Within minutes, Frank asked if we wanted to see him go, so he went out in the street, screamed “GO!!” and off Leroy went.  They have apparently been clocked at 19 mph as you can learn from this local news segment about the two of them.

That about sums it up

After hearing of Frank’s plan to run for congress, how he partied with Cyndi Lauper in the 80’s, that he was going on tour with his one man guitar set when his record came out in a month and how he wanted me to get a ramp into Bessie so I could be his tour bus, well, you get the picture.  Then the reporter who did the story stopped by with the weather girl for a visit and a drink at “the office”.  Then…

OK, that was 3:30 PM and I stayed out until about 2, so you can guess for yourself plenty more happenned, but I’ll stop rambling.  I was originally going to say that everyone should do Mardi Gras at least once in their life (well, if they’re young, or young at heart and like to party) but I can tell you this, I’ll be going back for another.
